traveler: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart (Joannes Chrysostomus Wolfgangus Theophilus Mozart)
title: The Getreidegasse to the Shaft Grave: the Child Shown at Court, the Servant Dismissed, and the Unmarked Ground
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Salzburg, Getreidegasse 9: the birth
stops.date_confidence: attested. Date, house, and floor are given by the International Mozarteum Foundation and by Wikipedia, 'Mozart's Birthplace', which supplies the coordinate 47.80000 N, 13.04333 E. The research pool's chronology and geography lenses carried two different coordinates for this house, 47.7981/13.0450 and 47.7998/13.0464, both of which fall southeast of Getreidegasse 9; the Mozarteum museum pin is used here and the discrepancy is recorded in the report.
stops.campa: On the third floor of the Hagenauer house, above a grocer's shop on Salzburg's chief merchant street, Anna Maria Pertl bears her seventh child. Six of the seven do not live. This one and his sister Maria Anna, five years older and called Nannerl, do. The father is Leopold Mozart, violinist to the court of the prince-archbishop and author of a violin method that will be reprinted across Europe for a century. The city outside the window belongs to a churchman who rules it as a sovereign prince and keeps Leopold as one more musician of his household. He is born on 27 January 1756.
suggested_refs: The Mozart birthplace apartment at Getreidegasse 9, Salzburg, a house museum of the International Mozarteum Foundation since 1880

stops.name: Salzburg Cathedral: the baptismal register
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Latin baptismal entry of St Rupert's is the first document of his existence.
stops.campa: He is carried the short distance to the cathedral of St Rupert and entered in the Latin register as Joannes Chrysostomus Wolfgangus Theophilus Mozart. Theophilus is Greek for beloved of God. He will render it later as Amade, Amadeo, and Amadeus by turns, and sign himself Wolfgang Amade when he signs formally at all; the Latin Amadeus that the world eventually settled on is mostly the work of people writing about him after he was dead. Chrysostomus comes from the saint whose day it is. Wolfgangus comes from his mother's father. He is one day old.
suggested_refs: The baptismal register of Salzburg Cathedral, entry of 28 January 1756

stops.name: Munich, the Residenz: the children shown
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the trip and the court; the pool gives January 1762 without a day, so the day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: Leopold takes the two children to the Bavarian electoral court, six years old and ten, and shows them to Maximilian III. It is the first documented performance trip of a career that will be spent almost entirely on roads. Leopold has worked out what he has: a boy who plays and composes at an age for which no explanation but prodigy is available, and prodigy has a market and a short season. Nannerl at ten is by every contemporary account his equal at the keyboard.
suggested_refs: The Munich Residenz, the Bavarian electoral court of Maximilian III Joseph

stops.name: Schonbrunn: before the empress
stops.date_confidence: attested for the journey and the audience: German Wikipedia gives departure from Salzburg on 20 September 1762, arrival in Vienna on 6 October, presentation at Schonbrunn on 13 October. The research pool's chronology lens dated the court appearance to September 1762, which is the departure and not the audience; the correction is applied here. The lap-and-proposal anecdote is later court folklore, tagged R, unconfirmed against any contemporary source.
stops.campa: The family leaves Salzburg on 20 September, travels by Passau and Linz, and reaches Vienna on 6 October. A week later the children play at the summer palace before Maria Theresa, Francis I, and the imperial children. The empress receives them warmly; they are paid, and clothed in cast-off court dress cut down for children. What everyone remembers afterward is a story instead: that the boy slipped on the polished floor, that the eight-year-old Archduchess Marie Antoinette caught him, and that he announced he would marry her. No contemporary document records it.
suggested_refs: The court portraits of the Mozart children in imperial gala dress, painted after the 1762 Vienna visit
sources: German Wikipedia, 'Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart' (itinerary of the 1762 Vienna journey)

stops.name: Salzburg: the departure of 9 June 1763
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On 9 June the family sets out west with a servant and a hired carriage on a tour that is meant to last some months and will last three and a half years. Leopold has taken leave from the archbishop's service and will stretch it past all patience. The route as it unfolds runs through Munich, Augsburg, Schwetzingen, Frankfurt, Aachen, Brussels, Paris, London, The Hague, Amsterdam, Utrecht, Zurich, and Donaueschingen. The boy is seven years old on the morning the carriage leaves the Getreidegasse.
suggested_refs: Leopold Mozart's travel notes and expense books of the western tour, 1763-1766

stops.name: Paris: the first winter
stops.date_confidence: attested for the stay; the arrival day is the standard itinerary date rather than one I could confirm against a primary document. The coordinate is the atlas pin used for the city across existing files, kept here for the general Paris stop; the 1778 Paris stops in this file carry their own precise addresses.
stops.campa: The family reaches Paris in mid-November and stays the winter. Here the first music of Wolfgang's to be printed is engraved and sold, four sonatas for keyboard with violin accompaniment, the work of a seven-year-old and advertised as such. Leopold has been on the road five months and is learning the trade of managing a wonder, which consists of arriving, waiting for an audience, and selling what can be sold in the interval. The waiting is most of it. In Brussels the family had sat idle for weeks before Prince Charles of Lorraine found time to hear them play.
suggested_refs: The engraved Paris sonatas K. 6-9, the first published works, 1764

stops.name: Versailles: the table of Louis XV
stops.date_confidence: attested for the reception at the New Year; the detail of the boy standing at the queen's side and being fed from her hand is reported rather than documented, and is carried here as report.
stops.campa: On New Year's Day the children are received at the French court. The account that comes down has Wolfgang standing beside Queen Maria Leszczynska at the royal table, handed morsels by her, speaking German with her because she has it and the courtiers do not. The household pays in gold snuffboxes. The family accumulates a great many of them and can turn almost none into money, and Leopold keeps his inventory accordingly: the boxes, the watches and the rings on their own page, the concert takings in cash on another.
suggested_refs: Leopold Mozart's inventory of gifts received on the western tour, snuffboxes, watches, and rings

stops.name: London: the court of George III and Johann Christian Bach
stops.date_confidence: attested for the fifteen-month stay and the Bach acquaintance. The knee-and-alternating-bars scene is a widely repeated report rather than a document. The lodging address in Chelsea is traditional attribution among several London addresses of the stay and is treated with caution.
stops.campa: Fifteen months in London, the longest halt of the tour. George III and Queen Charlotte receive the family more than once and the king sets the boy sight-reading at the keyboard. Johann Christian Bach, youngest son of the Leipzig cantor and the most fashionable composer in England, takes the eight-year-old on his knee and plays with him a bar at a time, turn and turn about. It is the decisive musical friendship of the childhood, and Italian opera, which Bach writes and London hears, enters the boy's ear here. In lodgings in Chelsea, while Leopold lies ill and the children are kept from the keyboard, Wolfgang writes his first symphonies.
suggested_refs: The Chelsea lodging on the site of 180 Ebury Street, where the first symphonies were written
The London sketchbook of 1764-65

stops.name: The Hague, the Binnenhof: both children ill
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Dutch illnesses; the pool gives 1765-1766 without a month, so the month and day default. The last rites for Nannerl are reported rather than documented.
stops.campa: In the Dutch months both children fall dangerously ill, Nannerl first and so gravely that she is thought to have been given the last rites, then Wolfgang after her. They recover. The tour goes on to Amsterdam and Utrecht and then turns for home: Paris again, Dijon, Lyon, Geneva, Zurich in the autumn of 1766, Donaueschingen, Munich. The family re-enters Salzburg on 29 November 1766, three and a half years after leaving it. Wolfgang is ten years old and has spent more than a third of his life in a carriage.
suggested_refs: The Binnenhof and the Dutch stadtholder's court at The Hague, autumn 1765

stops.name: Olomouc, the deanery: the smallpox
stops.date_confidence: attested for the illness and the shelter; the day is the standard date and is not one I confirmed against a primary source. The research pool called the house an archbishop's palace, which is anachronistic: Olomouc was a bishopric until 1777. German Wikipedia has both children take the disease, not Wolfgang alone. Coordinate moved from the town centre to the cathedral and deanery quarter.
stops.campa: The family goes to Vienna in the autumn of 1767 for an imperial wedding and finds a smallpox epidemic waiting. They leave for Moravia to escape it and both children take the disease anyway. At Olomouc they lodge first at the inn of the Black Eagle, then are taken into the deanery by Count Leopold Anton Podstatsky, dean of the cathedral chapter, who nurses them through it. The town is a bishopric in 1767, not yet the archbishopric it becomes ten years later, and the house that shelters them is a cathedral dean's.
suggested_refs: The cathedral deanery at Olomouc, house of Count Leopold Anton Podstatsky

stops.name: Vienna, the palais on the Landstrasse: Bastien und Bastienne
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The commission and the work are attested; the staging in Mesmer's garden theatre rests on Georg Nikolaus Nissen's posthumous biography alone, with no contemporary programme, letter, or score annotation, and Nissen himself reported finding no proof. The commission is also claimed for Mesmer's cousin Joseph Conrad Mesmer. Earliest securely documented staging is Berlin, 1890. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from mesmer.journey.json.
stops.campa: Back in Vienna the twelve-year-old writes a Singspiel, Bastien und Bastienne, a small pastoral about a shepherdess, a shepherd, and a village magician who cures love by pretending to conjure. Tradition, first written down by Constanze's second husband long after everyone concerned was dead, puts its first performance in the garden theatre of Franz Anton Mesmer, physician of animal magnetism, at his palais on the Landstrasse. Nissen looked for proof and found none. Twenty-two years later Mozart will put a mesmeric magnet on stage in Cosi fan tutte and have a fake doctor wave it over two men pretending to be poisoned.
suggested_refs: Franz Anton Mesmer's palais and garden at Rasumofskygasse 29, Vienna
Andrew Steptoe, 'Mozart, Mesmer and Cosi fan tutte', Music and Letters
sources: mesmer.journey.json, 'Vienna, the palais on the Landstrasse'
Andrew Steptoe, 'Mozart, Mesmer and Cosi fan tutte' (jstor.org/stable/735887)

stops.name: Rome, the Sistine Chapel: the Miserere
stops.date_confidence: attested by Leopold's own letter written within days; the day given is the Holy Week date in standard chronologies. Later retellings inflate the papal secrecy and the claim of a single unaided hearing. The Golden Spur investiture in July is attested separately and is folded into this stop.
stops.campa: In Holy Week the fourteen-year-old hears Gregorio Allegri's Miserere sung in the Sistine Chapel and writes it out afterward from memory, correcting his copy at a second hearing. Leopold reports the feat home within days of it happening; everything that makes the story famous, the papal ban on copying, the threat of excommunication, the single hearing, thickens around it later. In July the pope, Clement XIV, makes him a Knight of the Golden Spur. The order entitles him to be styled Signor Cavaliere, and for a season he signs himself so.
suggested_refs: The Order of the Golden Spur conferred on Mozart by Clement XIV, Rome, July 1770
sources: International Mozarteum Foundation, digital documentary edition (dme.mozarteum.at)

stops.name: Bologna, the Accademia Filarmonica: the examination
stops.date_confidence: attested for the admission and for the summer study with Martini; the surviving exercise sheet showing correction in another hand is documented in the academy's own archive.
stops.campa: Padre Giovanni Battista Martini, the Franciscan who is Europe's leading authority on counterpoint and keeps its largest music library, takes the boy as a pupil through the summer. In October the Accademia Filarmonica sets him the statutory examination, an antiphon to be set in strict church style, the candidate locked alone in a room with it. The surviving sheets show a hand other than his correcting the work. He is admitted anyway; the academy's minimum age of twenty is waived without recorded discussion. He is fourteen.
stops.quote: I can't possibly write better, for my pen is only fit to write music and not a letter.
stops.quote_source: Letter to his sister Maria Anna (Nannerl) Mozart, Bologna, 4 August 1770, in The Letters of Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, trans. Lady Wallace (1866), Vol. I, Letter 19
suggested_refs: The Accademia Filarmonica archive at Bologna, holding Mozart's 1770 examination exercise
Padre Martini's music library, now the Museo internazionale e biblioteca della musica
sources: International Mozarteum Foundation, digital documentary edition (dme.mozarteum.at)
Project Gutenberg ebook 5307, Letters of Mozart, Letter 19 (fetched and verified verbatim)

stops.name: Milan, the Teatro Regio Ducale: Mitridate
stops.date_confidence: attested. The research pool placed this theatre near Piazza della Scala at 45.4676/9.1897, which is La Scala, a separate later building inaugurated in 1778. The Teatro Regio Ducale was a wing of the ducal palace beside the cathedral at 45.4632/9.19114 and burned on 25 February 1776; the corrected pin is used here.
stops.campa: The opera is commissioned for the Milan carnival and the fourteen-year-old writes it against resistance from singers who do not want their arias out of a boy. He rewrites what they demand rewritten, over and over, and keeps the voices flattered. Mitridate, re di Ponto opens on the second day of Christmas in the theatre that is a wing of the ducal palace beside the cathedral, and runs more than twenty performances. No Italian court offers him a post. The building burns on 25 February 1776.
suggested_refs: The site of the Teatro Regio Ducale, Milan, destroyed by fire 25 February 1776
sources: International Mozarteum Foundation, digital documentary edition (dme.mozarteum.at)

segments.name: Salzburg Service and the Road Away

stops.name: Milan: Lucio Silla and the post that never comes
stops.date_confidence: attested for both premieres, Ascanio in Alba on 17 October 1771 and Lucio Silla on 26 December 1772. Maria Theresa's advice to Archduke Ferdinand against employing itinerant musicians is documented in her correspondence and is the standard explanation for the failed appointment; the wording is paraphrased here rather than quoted.
stops.campa: Two more Italian journeys follow and two more Milan operas, Ascanio in Alba for an archducal wedding in 1771 and Lucio Silla two years later on the same day of the year as Mitridate. Both succeed. Neither produces a post. Maria Theresa, written to by her son Ferdinand about taking the young Mozart into his household, advises him against burdening himself with musicians who go about the world like beggars. The three Italian journeys end here, and Italy, which had been the entire plan since he was thirteen, is finished.
stops.quote: This is famous for a composer - it inspires so many fine thoughts.
stops.quote_source: Letter to his sister Nannerl, Milan, 23 August 1771, in The Letters of Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, trans. Lady Wallace (1866), Letter 33; written of the violinist above, the violinist below, and the singing-master and oboist next door
suggested_refs: Maria Theresa's letter to Archduke Ferdinand on the employment of the Mozarts, 1771
sources: International Mozarteum Foundation, digital documentary edition (dme.mozarteum.at)
Project Gutenberg ebook 5307, Letters of Mozart, Letter 33 (fetched and verified verbatim)

stops.name: Salzburg, the Tanzmeisterhaus: Konzertmeister to Colloredo
stops.date_confidence: attested for the return from Italy and the Salzburg employment; the family's move to the Tanzmeisterhaus on the Hannibalplatz, now Makartplatz 8, is dated 1773 in the sources without a day.
stops.campa: The family moves across the river to a larger house on the Hannibalplatz, eight rooms and a dancing-master's hall, and Wolfgang settles into salaried employment with the prince-archbishop Hieronymus Colloredo as Konzertmeister. He is seventeen. For the next four years he produces what the court requires: masses and litanies for the cathedral, serenades for university graduations, symphonies, concertos for the violin he plays well and does not enjoy playing. Colloredo pays little and grants leave less freely than Leopold's long absences had taught the household to expect.
suggested_refs: The Tanzmeisterhaus, Makartplatz 8, Salzburg, the Mozart family residence from 1773

stops.name: Munich: out of the archbishop's service
stops.date_confidence: attested. Departure from Salzburg 23 September 1777, arrival in Munich within days; the letter quoted is dated at Munich, 26 September 1777, and was verified verbatim in Project Gutenberg ebook 5307.
stops.campa: He asks Colloredo for leave to travel and is refused. Father and son together tender their resignations; the archbishop discharges Wolfgang and keeps Leopold, who cannot afford to go. So the twenty-one-year-old leaves Salzburg on 23 September with his mother in the carriage instead of his father, the first journey of his life without Leopold in it. Three days later he is in Munich, sounding out the Elector Karl Theodor for a post and writing home about how it feels to be out.
stops.quote: My head feels as light as a feather since I got away from that chicanery.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Leopold Mozart, Munich, 26 September 1777, in The Letters of Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, trans. Lady Wallace (1866), Letter 60
suggested_refs: The Mozart-Leopold correspondence of the 1777-1779 journey, the densest surviving stretch of the family letters
sources: Project Gutenberg ebook 5307, Letters of Mozart, Letter 60 (fetched and verified verbatim)

stops.name: Augsburg, St Anna's: the organ and the Basle
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Augsburg stay and the cousin; the day is the standard date rather than one confirmed from a primary source. Whether the relationship with Maria Anna Thekla Mozart was also sexual is unproven and is left unresolved.
stops.campa: In his father's birth city he tries the organ at St Anna's and gives a concert to a thin house. He also finds his cousin Maria Anna Thekla Mozart, two years younger, whom he calls the Basle. The letters he writes her over the next years are punning, scatological, obscene, and plainly delighted, a register that appears nowhere else in his correspondence and that nineteenth-century editors quietly cut out of the published volumes. What else the relationship was, the record does not say. The letters are the only evidence and they do not settle it.
suggested_refs: The Basle letters to Maria Anna Thekla Mozart, restored uncensored in Robert Spaethling's Mozart's Letters, Mozart's Life (2000)
sources: Moller, 'Do features of Mozart's letter-writing style indicate the presence of a neuropsychiatric disorder?' (pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24337967)

stops.name: Mannheim: the electoral orchestra
stops.date_confidence: attested for the arrival date and the winter stay.
stops.campa: Mannheim keeps the best orchestra in Europe, drilled to a precision other courts cannot buy, famous for its wind players and for a swelling crescendo that people travelled to hear once. Mozart stays the winter and his orchestral imagination is rebuilt around it: winds as voices carrying the argument rather than filling the middle, dynamics as an event in themselves. He also meets the Webers, a family of copyist, prompter, and four daughters, and falls in love with the second, the soprano Aloysia. Leopold, reading about it at home in Salzburg, orders him to Paris.
suggested_refs: The Mannheim court orchestra under Christian Cannabich, and the Mannheim school's wind writing

stops.name: Paris, the Salle des Cent Suisses: the Paris Symphony
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date and the work. The research pool located the Concert Spirituel at the Palais-Royal, which is wrong: Wikipedia, 'Concert Spirituel', places it for many years in the Salle des Cent Suisses inside the Tuileries palace, moving only in 1784 to the Salle des Machines, also in the Tuileries. Venue and coordinate corrected here.
stops.campa: The Concert Spirituel plays in the Hall of the Hundred Swiss Guards inside the Tuileries palace, and on 18 June it gives the symphony Mozart has written for it, scored for the largest orchestra he has yet had at his disposal, clarinets included. He has built the first movement to catch a French audience and it catches them. The rest of the Paris months are thin: pupils he does not want, no post, a city that had adored him at seven and does not much notice him now. The one commission of substance comes from a duke who plays the flute and has a daughter who plays the harp, and he writes a concerto for the pair of them.
suggested_refs: Symphony No. 31 in D, K. 297, the Paris, premiered at the Concert Spirituel 18 June 1778

stops.name: Paris, rue du Sentier: his mother dies
stops.date_confidence: attested; the death is documented and the two letters of that night survive. The lodging street is the standard attribution.
stops.campa: Anna Maria Mozart has been ill for weeks in the lodgings her son found for them and dies here on the evening of 3 July, fifty-seven years old, with only Wolfgang in the room. He does not send the news to his father straight. He writes twice that night: to Leopold, that his mother is very ill and he should prepare himself; and to the Salzburg family friend Abbe Joseph Bullinger, the truth, asking him to break it. She is buried the next day from the parish church of Saint-Eustache. Her grave, like her son's thirteen years later, is not preserved as a marked place.
stops.quote: Mourn with me! This has been the most melancholy day of my life; I am now writing at two o'clock in the morning.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Abbe Joseph Bullinger, Paris, 3 July 1778, in The Letters of Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, trans. Lady Wallace (1866)
suggested_refs: The church of Saint-Eustache, Paris, from which Anna Maria Mozart was buried on 4 July 1778
sources: Project Gutenberg ebook 5307, Letters of Mozart (fetched and verified verbatim)
Anderson, The Letters of Mozart and His Family

stops.name: Mannheim: on the road home
stops.date_confidence: attested for the letter and the return leg. The quoted wording is Lady Wallace's and differs from the widely circulated compression, 'As I love Mannheim, Mannheim loves me', which is a later editor's shortening.
stops.campa: Ordered home, he takes four months over a journey of weeks. He stops at Mannheim, where the elector's court has removed to Munich and taken the orchestra with it, and writes to Salzburg that something may yet be found for him in the town anyway. Leopold's letters come back sharper each time. He reaches Salzburg in the middle of January, without an appointment. At Munich on the way, in December, he had found Aloysia Weber engaged at the court theatre and grown, and she had refused him.
stops.quote: Just as I love Mannheim, so Mannheim loves me; and, though of course I don't know it positively, still I do think it possible that I may get an appointment here.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Leopold Mozart, Mannheim, 12 November 1778, in The Letters of Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, trans. Lady Wallace (1866)
suggested_refs: The Mannheim court's removal to Munich in 1778 on Karl Theodor's accession to Bavaria
sources: Project Gutenberg ebook 5307, Letters of Mozart (fetched and verified verbatim)

stops.name: Salzburg Cathedral: court and cathedral organist
stops.date_confidence: attested for the appointment and the salary of 450 florins.
stops.campa: He takes the post of court and cathedral organist at four hundred and fifty florins a year, better paid than the Konzertmeister place he walked out of and more plainly a servant's. For two years he plays the cathedral organ and writes what the cathedral and the court ask for. He is twenty-three, living again in the house his mother left with him and did not return to. The family letters, which carry the record of the travelling years, all but stop: father and son are under one roof.
suggested_refs: The organ of Salzburg Cathedral and the Salzburg church works of 1779-1780

stops.name: Munich, the Cuvillies Theatre: Idomeneo
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The Bavarian court commissions a serious opera for the carnival and he writes the largest thing he has yet attempted: a Cretan king who has promised the sea god the first man he meets ashore, and meets his son. Into the Italian forms he pours what Mannheim taught him, winds carrying the drama and a chorus used as French tragedy uses one. He rehearses it in the small rococo theatre of the Residenz, arguing by post with Leopold over every cut. It opens on 29 January. He is twenty-five, and when the run closes he does not go home.
suggested_refs: The Cuvillies Theatre in the Munich Residenz, where Idomeneo was first staged
sources: International Mozarteum Foundation, digital documentary edition (dme.mozarteum.at)

stops.name: Vienna, the Deutschordenshaus: dismissed
stops.date_confidence: attested for the rupture and the dismissal, which run from 9 May to 8 June 1781. The kick from Count Arco is reported in Mozart's own letter and by no independent witness; it is his account of what happened to him, not a corroborated fact.
stops.campa: Colloredo summons his household to Vienna for the accession celebrations and lodges his musicians in the house of the Teutonic Order on the Singerstrasse, where Mozart eats at a table below the valets and is forbidden to play for anyone but the archbishop. He asks to be released, repeatedly, through May and into June. On the eighth of June the chief steward, Count Karl Joseph Arco, puts him out of the room with, in Mozart's own telling, a kick in the arse. Nobody else who was present wrote anything down. He stays on in Vienna and takes lodgings with the Weber family.
suggested_refs: The Deutschordenshaus on the Singerstrasse, Vienna, quarters of the Salzburg court musicians in 1781
sources: Anderson, The Letters of Mozart and His Family, letters of May and June 1781

stops.name: Vienna, the Burgtheater: Die Entfuhrung aus dem Serail
stops.date_confidence: attested for the premiere. Coordinate corrected: the eighteenth-century Burgtheater stood on Michaelerplatz adjoining the Hofburg, not on the Ringstrasse, where the present building dates only from 1888. The research pool's 48.2065/16.3663 matches neither. Joseph II's 'too many notes' remark reaches us only through Niemetschek's later biography and is tagged R.
stops.campa: The emperor Joseph II wants German opera in his court theatre and gets it: a Singspiel about a Spanish nobleman, a Turkish pasha, and a servant who cannot keep his mouth shut, with janissary drums and cymbals in the pit. The emperor is supposed to have told him it had too many notes; that remark is first printed by Niemetschek at Prague in 1798, seven years after Mozart's death, and nobody who was in the room left an account of it. The piece succeeds at once, travels, and makes Mozart's name across the German-speaking lands.
suggested_refs: Franz Niemetschek, Leben des k. k. Kapellmeisters Wolfgang Gottlieb Mozart (Prague, 1798), source of the 'too many notes' anecdote

stops.name: Vienna, St Stephen's: the marriage to Constanze Weber
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Mozarteum and by the cathedral record; Leopold's written consent arriving the day after the wedding is attested.
stops.campa: Three weeks after the Entfuhrung he marries Constanze Weber in the cathedral, third of the four Weber daughters, younger sister of the Aloysia who refused him in Munich. Leopold's consent has been asked for, withheld, and asked for again. The couple marry without it. It arrives from Salzburg by post the day after the wedding. They will have six children in nine years and bury four of them, beginning with Raimund Leopold, born in the following June and dead in August before he was nine weeks old.
suggested_refs: The marriage register of St Stephen's Cathedral, Vienna, 4 August 1782

stops.name: Vienna, Domgasse 5: the house of the quartets
stops.date_confidence: attested for the residence 1784-1787, for Carl Thomas's birth on 21 September 1784, and for his death without issue in 1858. Haydn's remark to Leopold is reported in the family correspondence tradition and is not independently verified here; it is carried as report.
stops.campa: The apartment behind the cathedral, up four flights off the Domgasse, is the largest and most expensive he ever rents. Here Carl Thomas is born in September 1784 and survives, one of the two out of six children who will; he ends as a government accounting official in Milan and dies without children in 1858. Here Mozart writes Le nozze di Figaro and three of the six string quartets he dedicates to Joseph Haydn. Haydn, visiting, is said to have told Leopold to his face that the son was the greatest composer he knew of. It is the only one of his Viennese lodgings still standing.
suggested_refs: Mozarthaus Vienna, Domgasse 5, the sole surviving Mozart residence in the city

stops.name: Vienna, Zur Wohltatigkeit: the initiation
stops.date_confidence: attested for both dates, initiation 14 December 1784 and Fellow Craft 7 January 1785, per the King's College London Mozart material-culture database. The exact lodge premises are not fixed in the surviving record, so the coordinate marks central Vienna rather than a building.
stops.campa: On the fourteenth of December he is initiated as an Entered Apprentice in the lodge Beneficence; where the premises stood is not fixed in the surviving record. Three weeks later he takes the Fellow Craft degree in True Concord, the largest and most learned lodge in Vienna, presided over by the mineralogist Ignaz von Born, and he is a Master within months. Leopold, visiting the following spring, is initiated himself. Mozart writes for the lodges for the rest of his life: funeral music, cantatas, songs for the opening and the closing of the work.
suggested_refs: The lodge Zur wahren Eintracht under Ignaz von Born, and the 1785 consolidation into Zur neugekronten Hoffnung
sources: King's College London, Mozart material-culture database, 'True Concord' masonic lodge (mmc.kdl.kcl.ac.uk)
Museum of Freemasonry, 'Was Mozart a Freemason?'

stops.name: Vienna, the Burgtheater: Le nozze di Figaro
stops.date_confidence: attested for the premiere and the nine-performance first season. The Prague reception is attested; Mozart's remark that nothing is talked of but Figaro is paraphrased here from his January 1787 letter rather than quoted. Burgtheater coordinate corrected as above.
stops.campa: Beaumarchais's play is banned in Vienna, and the librettist Lorenzo Da Ponte gets the opera past the imperial censor by cutting the count's politics and leaving his conduct. What remains is a servant outwitting his master over the right to a wife, sung. It runs nine performances in its first Vienna season, which is respectable and not more than that. In Prague that winter it takes the whole city; Mozart, who goes there in January to see it, writes home that nothing is talked of, played, sung, or whistled but Figaro.
suggested_refs: Lorenzo Da Ponte's censored adaptation of Beaumarchais's La folle journee for the Vienna stage
sources: International Mozarteum Foundation, digital documentary edition (dme.mozarteum.at)

stops.name: Salzburg: the death of Leopold
stops.date_confidence: attested for the death and for Wolfgang's absence from the funeral; the sources do not give a reason and none is supplied here. The quoted letter is Wallace's translation, verified in the Internet Archive scan of Volume II, Letter 243. Emily Anderson's better-known English wording of the same passage could not be checked against an Anderson edition and is deliberately not used.
stops.campa: Leopold Mozart dies at the Tanzmeisterhaus, sixty-eight years old, having spent his life first making his son and then failing to govern him. Wolfgang is in Vienna and does not come; the record does not say why, and the estate is settled by correspondence with Nannerl. Six weeks earlier, on hearing that his father was gravely ill, he had written him a letter about death that has been quoted ever since, in English translations that differ from one another more than the people quoting them tend to notice.
stops.quote: As death (when closely considered) is the true goal of our life, I have made myself so thoroughly acquainted with this good and faithful friend of man, that not only has its image no longer anything alarming to me, but rather something most peaceful and consolatory.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Leopold Mozart, Vienna, 4 April 1787, in The Letters of Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, trans. Lady Wallace (1866), Vol. II, Letter 243 (archive.org, lettersofwolfgan02moza)
suggested_refs: The Wallace and Anderson English editions of the 4 April 1787 letter, which render the same German differently
sources: Lady Wallace, The Letters of Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, Vol. II, Letter 243 (archive.org OCR, fetched and verified verbatim)

segments.name: Prague, the Debts, and the Last Year

stops.name: Prague, the Estates Theatre: Don Giovanni
stops.date_confidence: attested for the premiere. Coordinate corrected: Wikipedia gives 50.08611, 14.42389 for the Estates Theatre; the research pool's 50.0865/14.4278 lies about 300 m east. The Kucharz remark is a secondhand report of speech, tagged R, and is cited to Kerst and Krehbiel rather than to Niemetschek, whose volume does not carry it.
stops.campa: Prague, which had taken Figaro as Vienna did not, commissions the next opera and gets a libertine dragged down to hell by a stone statue, with a comic servant keeping the list of his master's women. Da Ponte writes the words. The premiere is put off twice; the overture is finished at the last moment. Mozart lodges outside the city with the singer Josefa Duskova and her husband at their villa at Bertramka, where the garden keeps a tradition that he composed between turns at skittles.
stops.quote: It is a mistake to think that the practice of my art has become easy to me. I assure you, dear friend, no one has given so much care to the study of composition as I. There is scarcely a famous master in music whose works I have not frequently and diligently studied.
stops.quote_source: Reported remark to the conductor Johann Baptist Kucharz, who led the Don Giovanni rehearsals at Prague in 1787, in Friedrich Kerst, Mozart: The Man and the Artist, as Revealed in His Own Words, trans. Henry Edward Krehbiel (1906), no. 4
suggested_refs: The Estates Theatre, Prague, the house where Don Giovanni first played
Villa Bertramka at Smichov, the Duskova house outside the city
sources: Project Gutenberg ebook 4042, Kerst/Krehbiel, no. 4 (fetched and verified verbatim)

stops.name: Vienna: the three symphonies and the letters to Puchberg
stops.date_confidence: attested for the appointment as k. k. Kammermusicus in December 1787 at 800 florins, for the three catalogue entries of summer 1788, and for the start of the Puchberg loan letters that year. The absence of any documented lifetime performance of the three symphonies is a gap in the record, not a claim that they were never played.
stops.campa: In December 1787 the emperor makes him chamber composer at eight hundred florins a year, succeeding Gluck, and what the post actually requires is dance music for the court balls. In the summer of 1788 he enters three symphonies in his own catalogue within a few weeks of each other: E flat, G minor, and the C major that a later century calls the Jupiter. No performance of any of them in his lifetime is on record. In the same months he begins writing to Michael Puchberg, a brother in the lodge and a textile merchant, asking for money. He does not stop.
suggested_refs: The Puchberg loan letters, 1788-1791
Dexter Edge, 'Mozart and Finances', in Mozart in Context (Cambridge University Press)
sources: Dexter Edge, 'Mozart and Finances', Mozart in Context (cambridge.org)

stops.name: Leipzig, the Thomaskirche: the northern journey
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction for the organ scene, which survives in Bach-circle memoir rather than in any contemporary letter, and which I could not confirm against a primary source. The journey itself, Prague, Dresden, Leipzig, Potsdam, Berlin, with Prince Karl Lichnowsky, is attested, as is the modest documented financial return.
stops.campa: Travelling north with Prince Karl Lichnowsky through Prague and Dresden, he stops at the church where Johann Sebastian Bach was cantor for twenty-seven years and, the Leipzig memory holds, plays the organ until the choir gather round the bench to watch his feet. The journey goes on to Potsdam and Berlin and the court of Frederick William II, in search of commissions or a post. When Dexter Edge counts what the trip actually brought in, it is far less than the legend of lavish Prussian patronage that grew up around it afterward. He is home by June, and the letters to Puchberg resume.
suggested_refs: The Thomaskirche organ at Leipzig and the Bach-circle memoirs of Mozart's 1789 visit
sources: Dexter Edge, 'Mozart and Finances', Mozart in Context (cambridge.org)

stops.name: Vienna, the Burgtheater: Cosi fan tutte
stops.date_confidence: attested for the premiere and for the interruption by Joseph II's death on 20 February 1790. Frankfurt in October 1790 is attested as a self-financed journey; it is folded into this stop rather than given its own.
stops.campa: The third Da Ponte opera opens at the end of January: two officers, a wager on their fiancees, false Albanian moustaches, a maid impersonating a mesmerist doctor with a magnet, and the demonstration that both women can be had. It plays five times. Then the emperor Joseph II dies on the twentieth of February and the theatres shut for mourning. It resumes in the summer for five more performances and stops. In October, hoping to be noticed by the new court, Mozart pays his own way to Frankfurt for the coronation of Leopold II.
suggested_refs: The Frankfurt coronation of Leopold II, October 1790, attended by Mozart at his own risk
sources: Dexter Edge, 'Mozart and Finances', Mozart in Context (cambridge.org)

stops.name: Prague, the Estates Theatre: La clemenza di Tito
stops.date_confidence: attested. Flagged: an automated extraction of the Wikipedia article rendered this premiere as 6 December 1791, which is impossible, since Mozart is dead on 5 December. The coronation-opera date of 6 September 1791 is the well-documented one and is used here. Estates Theatre coordinate corrected as at the Don Giovanni stop.
stops.campa: Leopold II is crowned King of Bohemia and the Bohemian estates want an opera for the occasion. Mozart takes the commission in the middle of writing the Zauberflote, hands Metastasio's sixty-year-old libretto to Caterino Mazzola to be cut from three acts to two and modernised, and delivers the score in something like eighteen days. It opens on the coronation night before an audience that has come for a coronation. He is back in Vienna within the fortnight, finishing the other opera.
suggested_refs: Caterino Mazzola's reduction of Metastasio's La clemenza di Tito for the 1791 Prague coronation
sources: International Mozarteum Foundation, digital documentary edition (dme.mozarteum.at)

stops.name: Vienna, the Theater auf der Wieden: Die Zauberflote
stops.date_confidence: attested for the premiere date and for Mozart conducting early performances. Coordinate corrected to Wikipedia's 48.19778, 16.36611 for the Theater auf der Wieden; the research pool's figure sat about 120 m west. The casting of Josepha Hofer as the Queen of the Night and Schikaneder as Papageno is standard and was not confirmed from the fetched source.
stops.campa: Emanuel Schikaneder runs a suburban theatre in the Freihaus complex outside the city walls, for an audience that pays at the door, and he writes and stages a fairy opera with machines, a serpent, a bird-catcher, trials by fire and water, and a temple of priests whose rites anyone who has sat in a Vienna lodge would recognise on sight. Mozart conducts the first performances himself. Schikaneder plays Papageno. The Queen of the Night is sung by Josepha Hofer, Constanze's eldest sister.
suggested_refs: The Freihaus-Theater auf der Wieden and Schikaneder's troupe
The 1791 libretto of Die Zauberflote with its Masonic imagery
sources: International Mozarteum Foundation, digital documentary edition (dme.mozarteum.at)

stops.name: Vienna: the little Masonic cantata
stops.date_confidence: attested as the last completed entry in his own thematic catalogue. That the Requiem is absent from the catalogue follows from the catalogue itself; the anonymous commission through an intermediary is attested.
stops.campa: Eighteen days before he dies he conducts the Kleine Freimaurer-Kantate at the dedication of a new lodge temple, a short piece for tenor, two basses, and chorus, on a text about the light of this day. It is the last entry he makes in the thematic catalogue he has kept since 1784, in which he wrote out every finished work with its opening bars. The Requiem is not in it. He has been at work on that since the summer, commissioned through an intermediary by a man who would not give his name.
suggested_refs: Mozart's autograph thematic catalogue, 1784-1791, closing with K. 623

stops.name: Vienna, Rauhensteingasse: the death
stops.date_confidence: attested for the illness, the attending physicians, the hour of death, and the register diagnosis. The rehearsal of the Requiem at the bedside on 4 December and the reported deathbed words to Sophie Haibel are secondhand recollections set down years later and are tagged R.
stops.campa: He takes to his bed in the middle of November with fever, swelling of the hands and feet, pain, vomiting, and a rash. Thomas Franz Closset and Matthias von Sallaba attend him. On the evening of the fourth of December friends are remembered singing through parts of the unfinished Requiem at the bedside. He dies shortly before one in the morning on the fifth, aged thirty-five. The Vienna death register enters hitziges Frieselfieber, acute miliary fever, which names a set of symptoms and no disease. No autopsy is performed. Over a hundred modern diagnoses have been proposed since.
stops.quote: Stay with me to-night; you must see me die.
stops.quote_source: Reported deathbed words to his sister-in-law Sophie Haibel, nee Weber, Vienna, 5 December 1791, per her later letter to Georg Nikolaus Nissen; secondhand recollection recorded long after the fact
suggested_refs: Jan Hirschmann, 'What Killed Mozart?', JAMA Internal Medicine
Sophie Haibel's letter to Nissen on her brother-in-law's last day

stops.name: Vienna, St Stephen's: the consecration of the coffin
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to the chapel. The Mozarteum has the coffin consecrated at St Stephen's on 6 December at about three in the afternoon and transported that evening; the identification of the Crucifix chapel comes from later accounts rather than a contemporary document. The storm and the turned-back mourners are nineteenth-century additions.
stops.campa: The funeral is third class, the ordinary rate for a Viennese of his standing. The coffin is blessed at the Crucifix chapel on the north side of the cathedral at about three in the afternoon of the sixth and carried out to the cemetery that evening or the following day; the sources do not agree which. What survives from the week is a register line and an undertaker's charge. The storm, the mourners turned back at the gate, the hearse going on alone: all of that enters the story in the next century.
suggested_refs: The third-class funeral rate in Josephinist Vienna and the burial reforms of the 1780s

stops.name: St Marx Cemetery: the shaft grave
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the manner of burial. The date is contradicted between sources and the contradiction is left standing: the Mozarteum has the consecration and transport on 6 December, while Wikipedia's 'Death of Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart' states burial at St Marx on 7 December. The research pool's three lenses gave three different and mutually inconsistent coordinates for the cemetery; all three are wrong, and Wikipedia's 48.18278, 16.40167 is used here.
stops.campa: He is put into a common shaft outside the city walls with several other bodies, unmarked. That is what a third-class burial was; it is not what a pauper's burial was, and the two were confused within two generations. The plot is not recorded, and Viennese custom did not bring mourners to the graveside in any case. Graves in such a cemetery were dug over and reused on a fixed cycle of about ten years. St Marx stays in use until 1874 and is then closed to burials.
suggested_refs: St Marx Cemetery, Vienna, and the Josephinist shaft-grave practice for third-class burials

stops.name: Vienna: the Requiem finished in another hand
stops.date_confidence: attested for Eybler's abandoned attempt, Sussmayr's completion, and Walsegg's anonymous commission. The exact month of delivery is not fixed in the sources reached, so the day and month default.
stops.campa: Constanze needs the commission fee and the work has to be handed over complete. Joseph Eybler begins the completion and gives it up. Franz Xaver Sussmayr, Mozart's pupil, finishes it: he orchestrates what was sketched, writes the Sanctus and Benedictus outright, and brings back the opening music at the end. It goes to Count Franz von Walsegg, who had commissioned it anonymously through a messenger and meant to pass it off as his own memorial for his dead wife. What survives is partly Mozart, and no edition has ever settled which parts.
suggested_refs: The Sussmayr completion of the Requiem K. 626 and the Neue Mozart-Ausgabe critical report on it
sources: International Mozarteum Foundation, digital documentary edition (dme.mozarteum.at)

stops.name: St Marx Cemetery: the grave that cannot be found
stops.date_confidence: attested for both failed searches, Constanze's about seventeen years after the burial and Vincent Novello's in 1829, for the 1855 stone and its later removal to the Central Cemetery, and for the 1950 refurbishment by Florian Josephu-Drouot. The Zentralfriedhof cenotaph is undated in the source consulted; the 1891 year carried in the research pool is unsupported and is not asserted.
stops.campa: Constanze comes looking for the grave about seventeen years after the burial and cannot find it. Vincent Novello, the English musician and publisher, tries in 1829 and cannot find it either. A stone goes up at a presumed spot in 1855 and is later moved to the Central Cemetery, to stand among the composers' graves of honour over no body at all. A cemetery worker puts a memorial tablet in the gap it left at St Marx, added to over the years by contributors; what stands there now was refurbished in 1950 by the sculptor Florian Josephu-Drouot.
suggested_refs: The Mozart cenotaph among the musicians' graves of honour at the Vienna Central Cemetery
The St Marx memorial refurbished by Florian Josephu-Drouot, 1950

stops.name: Vienna: the poisoning that did not happen
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to the legend, which is what it is. There is no autopsy, no toxicology, no witness, and no document supporting a poisoning; the dramatic tradition from Pushkin in 1830 through Rimsky-Korsakov to Shaffer and Forman is attested as reception history. The date orders the segment at Pushkin's play.
stops.campa: Antonio Salieri, imperial Kapellmeister, colleague and competitor, ends his life in a Vienna asylum, and a rumour goes round that he confessed to poisoning Mozart. There is no autopsy, no toxicology, no witness, and no document. Pushkin writes a short play in 1830 in which the mediocrity murders the genius; Rimsky-Korsakov sets it as an opera at the end of that century; Peter Shaffer writes Amadeus in 1979 and Milos Forman films it in 1984. For most of the world that is now the story. Pushkin was born eight years after Mozart died.
suggested_refs: Pushkin, Mozart and Salieri (1830); Rimsky-Korsakov's opera (1897); Shaffer's Amadeus (1979) and Forman's film (1984)
sources: Handel and Haydn Society and Wisconsin Public Radio reception-history summaries, cited in the research dossier

stops.name: Leipzig: Kochel numbers the works
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Kochel-Verzeichnis of 1862, published by Breitkopf und Hartel at Leipzig, and for its continuing use through heavily revised editions. Tchaikovsky's Mozartiana of 1887 and its four borrowed works are documented, and the childhood orchestrion at Votkinsk is attested in tchaikovsky.journey.json; neither was re-verified here against a primary musicological source.
stops.campa: Ludwig von Kochel, a botanist and mineralogist with a private income, publishes a chronological catalogue of everything Mozart wrote, and from that year the works have numbers: K. 550 for the G minor symphony, K. 626 for the Requiem. Later editions reorder and reattribute a great deal and the numbers stay anyway, because by then they are how the music travels. Tchaikovsky, who first heard Mozart as a small child from a mechanical orchestrion in his father's house at Votkinsk, took four of them, K. 355, K. 592, K. 618, and K. 455, and made an orchestral suite of them called Mozartiana.
suggested_refs: The Kochel-Verzeichnis, first edition, Breitkopf und Hartel, Leipzig, 1862
The Neue Mozart-Ausgabe, Barenreiter, 1956-2007, 132 music volumes
Nadia Boulanger's Paris teaching, in which pupils sang Mozart to her in her last months
The 1993 Rauscher, Shaw, and Ky study in Nature and the 'Mozart effect' the press made of it
sources: Kochel catalogue, first edition, Breitkopf und Hartel, Leipzig, 1862
